item.title: How to live a life of awe
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
You don’t need to climb Kilimanjaro or see the Northern Lights to experience the benefits of awe. It’s everywhere if you look

- Video by the University of California and the Greater Good Science Center

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Awe is that transcendent feeling of stepping out of the quotidian and encountering something vast, mysterious and beyond your comprehension. The experience is a human universal, deeply rooted in our evolutionary history to make us feel connected to the world beyond us. And, as Dacher Keltner, distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, explores in this video, you don’t need to summit Mount Kilimanjaro, or head to the Arctic to see the Northern Lights, to enjoy its myriad rewards. Rather, awe is all around us, if you know where to look. Borrowing from ideas in his book Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life (2023), Keltner details how awe works, why it benefits us and how we can feel more of it in our everyday lives.

For more on how to find awe in your daily life, read this Psyche Guide.

item.title: Why romantic relationships matter more to men than to women
item.dc:creator: Iris Wahring
item.description:
For too long, men were told to be self-sufficient. The research shows they’re more likely to thrive in a loving couple

- by Iris Wahring

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
For centuries, the self-sufficient man who shuns romance has appeared as a kind of noble figure. ‘He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,’ wrote Francis Bacon in ‘Of Marriage and the Single Life’ (1625). ‘Certainly the best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from the unmarried or childless men.’ For Bacon, romantic relationships (and family) are impediments to a man becoming his best. Ralph Waldo Emerson devoted an entire essay, ‘Self-Reliance’ (1841), to the conviction that a man should stand apart from the crowd. ‘I shun father and mother and wife and brother, when my genius calls me,’ he wrote. Decades later, Rudyard Kipling reduced the idea to a single line: ‘He travels the fastest who travels alone.’

Such visions of self-sufficient masculinity endure in depictions of silent cowboys, wandering rōnin, desert hermits, elite soldiers, or libertines who treat love as a sport. Powered by their own strength and resilience, these men are domesticated only when circumstances or a determined partner finally insists on it. According to this view of masculinity, love is a welcome addition but never a need.

Women, on the other hand, have often been portrayed as being consumed by their desire for romantic relationships. Consider an often-quoted line from Lord Byron’s epic poem Don Juan (1819-24): love is just one part of a man’s life, Byron writes, but ‘tis woman’s whole existence’. If men can take or leave romance, the logic goes, then women must be the real romantics. They are the ones who fall harder and faster, and the ones who carry the emotional weight of a relationship.

But that’s not how things really work. As a researcher specialising in the psychology of romantic relationships, I have found that the evidence points the other way. In 2023 and 2024, I analysed more than 50 empirical studies and meta-analyses, revealing masculinity to be much more fragile than assumed. At every stage, from the first spark of attraction to the aftermath of a breakup, it is men who depend more on their romantic partners, for their happiness and, in measurable ways, for their survival.

To understand the disproportionate weight love carries for men, we must examine the trajectory of relationships, starting from the time when men are single and searching for a partner. On average, men consider finding a partner more important for their happiness than women do. When single, they are less satisfied with their relationship status and long for a partner more intensely. They also plunge into the feeling of falling in love more often and more quickly, and they experience unrequited love more frequently. Contrary to common expectations, men are typically the first to say ‘I love you’ in heterosexual relationships, according to a 2022 study led by Christopher Watkins from Abertay University in the UK, which surveyed participants across seven countries on three continents.

Once in a relationship, both partners usually benefit. Longitudinal research indicates that entering a romantic relationship itself is typically accompanied by increases in life satisfaction. Accordingly, couples tend to show higher levels of wellbeing, better mental and physical health, and even higher life expectancy than their single counterparts. Yet, all these benefits are more pronounced for men. For example, a 2020 meta-analysis by Yafeng Wang from Wuhan University in China and colleagues, involving data on marital status and mortality risk from 7.9 million individuals and 1.9 million deaths, found that unmarried women had a 22 per cent higher mortality risk than married women, but unmarried men even had a 46 per cent higher mortality risk than married men. So for the average man, being in a committed relationship is more decisive for how long they will live than it is for the average woman.

Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men

Many romantic relationships, however, end in a breakup and, if they do, this is typically initiated by women: among heterosexual couples, 60 to 70 per cent of breakups and divorces are initiated by women, according to studies in the US, Germany and Netherlands. The remaining 30 to 40 per cent are equally divided between mutual breakups and those initiated by men.

When the split happens, men suffer more. While a breakup is typically painful for women too, men tend to struggle more to find any positive aspects, such as relief or newfound independence, following a split. They are less likely to feel like they have learned something from the breakup. Men also tend to experience a sharper decline in life satisfaction, reporting higher levels of loneliness afterward and more frequently resorting to harmful coping mechanisms, such as alcohol and substance abuse.

Most alarmingly, the end of a relationship can be fatal. Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men. In a research paper in 2025, the men’s health expert Michael Wilson from the University of Melbourne and colleagues reviewed 75 prior studies on suicidality in men to find ‘the factors underpinning men’s suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and death by suicide following relationship breakdown’. They found that the risk of suicide was especially high during the separation period itself, nearly twice the odds seen in men who were already divorced (and more than four times as high as married men). For women, the suicide risk after a divorce or separation increases by a far smaller amount, if at all. For a significant number of men, losing a romantic relationship is, quite literally, a matter of life or death.

How did we arrive at a place where the supposedly ‘stronger’ gender longs intensely for a partner, relies more heavily on them for health and wellbeing, is more frequently left behind, and remains emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak? Multiple factors may play a role here.

Consider, for instance, the unequal distribution of household chores. Women spend substantially more time and effort doing unpaid care work, including both the execution and planning of tasks as part of home organisation. This unequal distribution of duties between heterosexual romantic partners is not without costs and is associated with lower levels of mental and physical health in women. However, after a breakup from a cohabitating partner, women tend to spend less time on household chores than before, leaving them with more time for enjoyable activities. Men, on the other hand, often suddenly lack the person who managed this workload, and may start spending more time on less enjoyable domestic activities.

Men, throughout their lives, are less likely to receive emotional support

A related practical factor that may shape the profound effect that romantic relationships have on the physical health and life expectancy of men is that women are more likely to remind their partners to go to the doctor than vice versa. Accordingly, while both men and women in romantic relationships tend to visit the doctor more often than their single counterparts, the difference between partnered and single individuals is more pronounced among men.

Child custody is another point. It is noteworthy that following a divorce, children tend to stay with their mothers in most cases, regardless of who initiates the breakup. That means fathers who walk away from a relationship not only lose their romantic partner but also risk a substantial reduction in contact with their children. The result is a compounding sense of loss, which mothers in the same position are far less likely to face.

However, the most robust and far-reaching explanation for why the ‘stronger’ gender is so much more emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak is intimacy: research consistently shows that men, throughout their lives, are less likely to receive emotional support.

All humans possess an innate need for intimacy. We want to confide in others, to feel secure, to be touched and held, and to know someone has our back. A central condition for experiencing emotional intimacy is receiving emotional support. Emotional support involves caring for another person’s wellbeing by understanding and appreciating them. Longitudinal and intervention research has proven that emotional support is a central resource for mental and physical health. The fundamental problem is that men often lack this support outside the boundaries of a romantic relationship. As shown in numerous studies, they tend to receive less emotional support from their friends and family than women do. Instead, men are more likely to view their romantic partners as their primary confidant.

This ‘intimacy deficit’ begins remarkably early. Even boys aged around 10 or 11 report opening up to friends far less than girls do. As they grow older, men are significantly less likely than women to have confidants they can turn to in times of trouble. To fill this gaping void, many men lean almost exclusively on the emotional support of their partners. Consequently, finding a partner represents a massive gain in emotional closeness for a man. And losing that partner can represent the loss of his entire emotional infrastructure.

We have created a paradox: forms of masculinity that forbid vulnerability guarantee an even higher level of vulnerability

The root of this isolation is the traditional male gender role. From early childhood, boys are socialised to view vulnerability as a weakness. Parents subtly enforce this: studies show that when talking to preschool-aged daughters as compared with sons, parents focus more on emotional experiences and react more positively to sadness.

By adolescence, boys have learned the lesson. They expect that opening up to friends will feel ‘weird’. Adult men go on to judge other men harshly when they show vulnerability, seeing it as a violation of traditional masculinity. A comprehensive meta-analysis led by the social psychologist Alice Eagly from Northwestern University in Illinois, including studies spanning from 1946 to 2018, shows that communal traits, like emotionality and nurturance, are still overwhelmingly attributed to women. Both men and women continue to view emotionality as a desirable trait in women, but an undesirable one in men.

Yet, beneath this stoic mask, men experience vulnerable emotions like sadness and fear just as frequently and intensely as women do. We have created a paradox: forms of masculinity that forbid vulnerability guarantee an even higher level of vulnerability. Because deep emotional connection is socially acceptable for men only within the confines of a romantic relationship, they are left utterly defenceless when they are single or when a relationship ends.

While the societal roles and expectations for women have expanded massively in recent decades, the template for masculinity has largely stagnated. We continue to raise boys who become men who are wholly dependent on romantic partners for their basic emotional needs. This is an unfair burden to place on women and is actively impairing the health and life expectancy of millions of men.

Everyone, regardless of gender, should have the capacity to lead a fulfilled, emotionally supported life without a romantic partner. To achieve this, we must rewrite the societal image of masculinity from the ground up. We need to dispel the myth of stoic self-reliance. We need to normalise emotional openness and platonic intimacy among men, to ensure they lead healthy, resilient lives that are no longer existentially dependent on a romantic partner.

This shift must be systemic. It begins with parents, who must be encouraged to raise sons to view emotional openness as a fundamental life skill rather than a weakness. In schools, the importance of emotionally close friendships must be explicitly taught, creating spaces where boys learn that vulnerability is a strength.

Furthermore, we need targeted, community-based programmes for adult men that foster connections beyond romance. A promising model is the ‘Men’s Shed’ movement, which originated in Australia and is now run in several other countries around the world. These community workshops provide a space where men, typically of retirement age, can work on practical projects and talk ‘shoulder to shoulder’ rather than face-to-face. Such informal settings bypass the stigma of traditional therapy, reducing social isolation and increasing wellbeing.

For centuries, men have been told that romantic relationships don’t matter that much and that self-sufficiency is the answer to all problems. The research tells a different story: love, it turns out, is never just a small part of a man’s life.

item.title: Dear Al Pacino
item.dc:creator: Joe Mullich
item.description:
I wrote my mother’s mad letters to celebrities. It was the only time we shared the same plane of reality

- by Joe Mullich

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
My mother paced the patio, working through that week’s crisis aloud. An office mate, she was certain, was a CIA operative sent to spy on her.

I paced back and forth with her, hoping to shift her attention by describing what happened in my third-grade class. When none of my attempts landed, I went to our mailbox to retrieve the monthly issue of Reader’s Digest. At age eight, I was in love with the English language. I tore open the magazine to a feature called ‘It Pays to Increase Your Word Power’, a list of 10 little-used words. The third item stunned me – ‘sesquipedalianism’. I laughed when I read the definition: using a big word when a small one would do.

Before I realised it, my mother was looming behind me, ever-present cigarette dangling from her mouth. Peering at the long, odd, winding word, she nodded with satisfaction.

‘Al Pacino would understand that word,’ she said. ‘We should write a letter to Al Pacino. He will be able to put a stop to this. And be sure to use that seis-qui-whatever word.’

‘You think Al Pacino would know sesquipedalianism?’

‘Without a doubt! He’s an artist. If we use it in the letter, he’ll know how serious we are.’

‘I’ll get my notebook.’

I ran to my room. It was always a big moment when my mother came out of her walking fits. The next few minutes were critical in how the rest of her day went. I grabbed a handful of the #2 pencils I always kept sharpened and at the ready.

Initially, my mother simply had me proofread the letters she sent to celebrities asking them to intervene in the vast and ever-expanding conspiracy that was orchestrated against her. We wrote to Neil Armstrong, Walter Cronkite, Sean Connery and many people I did not recognise. Over time, my edits to her letters became so extensive that she decided to just dictate her thoughts and let me compose the missives.

When I came back, she was sitting at the breakfast nook, hands clamped at the edges of the table so tightly her knuckles turned white. I sat across from her.

‘Go ahead,’ I said.

My mother’s ramblings seemed like radio static while she spoke, and I understood her paranoia only when I translated it onto the page

She took a deep drag from a cigarette. When she looked down at the notebook, with my crisply sharpened #2 pencil hovering over it, her eyes turned into slits. She contemplated how to describe the full array of the injustices against her. In such moments, I would wait silently, sometimes for a few seconds, sometimes for 15 minutes, until the dam burst. At some point, words and thoughts would tumble out of her in turbulent currents. Sometimes the thoughts would contradict and bounce off each other, which only increased the frenzy of her telling.

When she finished, her eyes would be glassy but then focus. ‘You think we have it?’ she asked.

‘I think we have it.’

She took a deep drag on her cigarette and then snuffed it out. ‘I need to go lay down. Let me know when it’s done.’

I never took actual notes when she spoke. I just doodled on the notebook. I had learned that my mother’s meaning was never in the words themselves but in-between the words, in the tone, in the pauses, in the way her voice raised and lowered. Random and wild thoughts would fly by me like objects swirling in a tornado.

Her word salad never made sense when she was speaking. However, when I paused to put the jumble into a letter, one stray fact would jump out to me, and immediately lead me to another stray fact, forging a connection I had not noticed until then. My mother’s ramblings seemed like radio static while she spoke, and I understood her paranoia only when I translated it onto the page. In the middle of the tornado that was her mind lurked an eerily calm coherence – one I could reach only by listening and writing my way to its centre.

When I finished the letter, I called to her. She came out of the bedroom and plopped herself on the Naugahyde seats, looking both fascinated and sceptical at the paper I held in my hands. Then I read it aloud:

Dear Mr Godfather Pacino.
Only you can help me! This is a FEDERAL matter. They plot against me. I am a single MOTHER with 3 small children. No one is on my side. The father (mama’s boy) does nothing. Please use your connections. I am begging you. All I want is what everyone wants, to be left in peace.
[signed]
You Will Know
PS You are very handsome! (wink, wink)

Stripped of the frantic energy in her voice, her plea made a kind of sense. She was always complaining about how her co-workers at the US Postal Service were ‘getting in her business’ and how her supervisors would ignore her complaints. I added the underlines, capitalisation and exclamation points because I knew from past letters that she particularly liked how they looked on the page.

‘How did you know all that?’ she asked.

‘You just told me.’

She was not one for affectionate hugs, although she would occasionally goose me or my brothers

She took the yellow legal paper and held it as though it was a Gideon Bible. I had the sense that my mother didn’t really understand what she thought until I wrote it down. When it was read back to her, the magnitude of the situation would awe her. At this moment, we had the deepest connection – perhaps the only true connection – we would have in my lifetime. She stared at the letter in amazement that her pain and suffering could be made comprehensible.

‘You understand!’ she said.

‘It’s really not complicated when you get to the heart of it.’

She tipped her cigarette to me in a kind of salute and gave my hand a squeeze, a gesture that shocked me. She was not one for affectionate hugs, although she would occasionally goose me or my brothers, jabbing a middle finger into our blue jeans as we passed by. ‘Better watch out,’ she would direct. We were all very careful before entering any long, cramped hallway to make sure she wasn’t on the other side.

‘This is an excellent letter,’ she said. ‘I can’t imagine how Al Pacino won’t want to get involved. We need to get him this letter asap!’

‘You think he can help?’

She chuckled at the foolishness of my question. ‘Oh, if Al Pacino wants to help, he can help, believe you me. The government isn’t afraid of the little people, like you and me. They piss on the little people. But if the Godfather speaks, they’ll listen.’

I dragged my chair to the closet where we kept the brooms and mops. I stood on the chair to reach the upper shelf, which held a stack of phone directories. I opened up to the P section. There was a long string of Pacinos: A. Pacino, Alberto Pacino, Albert Pacino. I picked one at random.

When I wrote ‘Mr Al Pacino’ on the envelope, she said: ‘No. Make it ‘Senor Al Pacino.’ And put a little wavy thing over the N.’

‘Why?’

‘He’s Italian.’

She wrote ‘personal and confidential’ at the bottom of the letter, added three exclamation points, and circled it twice. She never put her return address on the envelope – ‘for security reasons’. Mrs Bottomfield, the neighbour my mother frequently threatened to kill for spying on her, was watering her lawn. She froze in terror at the sight of my mother. However, my mother was in such a happy mood that she let out a boisterous ‘Good afternoon, Beverly!’ and waved at her nemesis. Mrs Bottomfield waved back warily and slowly backed into her house, peering at us through the screen door until we were a safe distance away.

We walked to the mailbox three streets over. My mother believed it was safer to use ‘anonymous mailboxes’.

After depositing the letter, my mother said: ‘Al Pacino is going to lose it when he gets that letter. All hell is going to break loose. They won’t know what hit them. Let’s go get some ice cream.’

I was in the bubble of her madness, but my notebook – my words – shielded me from becoming consumed

‘Thrifty?’ I said excitedly, referencing the nearby drugstore where they would let you sample several flavours of ice cream before choosing one.

‘You bet! Don’t mention any of this to your brothers. They wouldn’t understand like you do. Let’s keep it just between us.’

‘OK,’ I said.

Another day, another secret.

When I wrote the letters for my mother, it was the only time I felt we occupied the same plane of reality. I was in the bubble of her madness, but my notebook – my words – shielded me from becoming consumed. I cared about her, but I watched from a distance, and that distance made her trust me, if only for a few minutes since trust was not something she could extend to anyone for a long period. When I started to write a letter from her perspective, everything she said made perfect sense, and it made me sorry for what she was going through.

My mother always made Don Quixote relatable to me. If you saw windmills as hulking giants out to destroy you, tilting at them with a lance was survival, not folly. Everything makes sense if you find the proper angle to view it from.

I had always been a quiet child, who liked to keep to the edges of a room or sit under a table and listen to adults talk at a party. But sitting across from my mother in that breakfast nook, I understood for the first time what I actually was: a translator. My gift was being able to listen to people and understand what they said and what they actually meant. That was the moment I found my calling.

item.title: How to overcome task paralysis
item.dc:creator: Joe Wilner
item.description:
If you have ADHD or you’re stressed, tired and stuck, goal management training can help you get started and keep going

- by Joe Wilner

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
It’s Thursday afternoon and the report has been sitting unfinished since Tuesday. Not untouched. You’ve opened it and closed it four or five times now, but can’t seem to make any progress. There’s also the dental appointment you’ve been meaning to schedule since January, and the email you finished writing last week that’s still sitting in your drafts for some unnameable reason.

You’re not procrastinating as such, because that’s a choice – like when you put off the tax return to watch the game, knowing at some level that you’re trading tomorrow’s stress for tonight’s comfort. This is about situations that run the other way. You want to start. You’ve cleared the afternoon, closed the distracting tabs on your screen, told yourself today is the day, and still nothing moves.

That strange bind, being unable to begin something you genuinely want to do, is task paralysis. I’ve spent years as a therapist working with adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), who often experience this problem because of their difficulties with executive function – the ability to plan and execute tasks. But it’s not just people with ADHD who struggle in this way. Push anyone through enough stress, too little sleep, or too far past their limits, and the same executive function system can start to falter, causing task paralysis to set in.

Goal management training

For many of my clients with ADHD, the usual support tools like task planners rarely seemed to help. When I learned about goal management training (GMT), an evidence-based programme for strengthening executive function, it stood out right away as something different. It offered a toolkit with an actual sequence of steps and specific strategies for building relevant skills. I trained in GMT, worked it into my clinical sessions, and watched it help people finally bridge the gap between knowing what they want to do and doing it.

GMT originated in the 1990s, when the psychologist Ian Robertson developed it at Cambridge University for people recovering from brain injury, whose capacity to hold a goal and act on it had been compromised. They would know that a goal mattered, hold it in mind, and yet still drift the moment something more immediate tugged at them. Robertson later refined the approach with the neuroscientist Brian Levine, and the version clinicians use today grew out of their collaboration.

Whether you have ADHD or you’re struggling for other reasons, I’ve written this Guide to show you how to use GMT to help yourself. The approach includes four stages: stop, define the goal, list the steps, check (repeated as needed). I’ll explain each of these stages in turn, then add three more that I’ve come to rely on with clients. None of the stages are complicated on their own. What makes them work is repetition: the executive functions you’re leaning on can even get stronger the more you use them.

As you read through the steps, I suggest you keep one stuck task in your mind, whether it’s that unfinished report, the unsent email, or something else, and that you try putting each step to work on it.

item.title: Are you getting enough sun?
item.dc:creator: Hannah Seo
item.description:
The new book ‘In Defense of Sunlight’ argues that our concerns about the sun’s risks lead us to overlook its benefits

- by Hannah Seo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Like many people nowadays, I grew up learning to see the sun as a threat. Exposure to its rays meant consequences like premature wrinkles, sunspots and, of course, skin cancer. The Korean aunties I knew heeded this dogma with sunglasses, flared visor hats, parasols and sun sleeves. While I’ve never gone to such lengths, I internalised the message.

But in his latest book In Defense of Sunlight (2026), the journalist Rowan Jacobsen argues that the common aversion to the sun has gone too far. He lays out decades of research linking moderate amounts of outdoor sunlight exposure with various positive health outcomes. One especially surprising study – which followed almost 30,000 Swedish women over 20 years – suggested that avoiding sunlight was about as big a risk factor for death as smoking. Sunlight is thought to aid physical health by, among other things, stimulating the production of vitamin D as well as the release of compounds such as nitric oxide (which can lower blood pressure).

Then there are the mental health benefits. Sun on the skin helps the body release endorphins, its natural opioids, and might help protect against depression. And proper exposure to sunlight and darkness massages the circadian rhythm into regularity, improving sleep quality, which, in turn, benefits your wellbeing.

Of course, everything in moderation: we still need to protect ourselves from excessive sun and UV exposure (so don’t throw away your sunscreen). But Jacobsen’s writing has helped me see how too much fear of the sun might be harming rather than protecting my health.

Now, the trick is to strike a balance, which I’ve sought by listening to my body. This past summer I tried to embrace the sun, retreating to the shade when I felt overheated or overstimulated. Maintaining moderation takes some push and pull, but I try to follow Jacobsen’s bottom-line message: ‘Get sun. Not too much. Go outside.’

item.title: Portraits of another life: Nemo Gould
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Driven by childhood curiosity, a sculptor turns discarded objects into kinetic artworks that are the antidote to AI slop

- Video by Portraits of Another Life

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The kinetic sculptor Nemo Gould has had a lifelong fascination with taking things apart and putting them back together, one he traces to a discovery he made as a child: most things are held together by screws and, once these are undone, the pieces can be built into something new. That early impulse, which led him to dismantle everything from his GI Joes to household appliances, grew into a deep curiosity about machines and how they work. Eventually, it became his art: discarded objects rebuilt into machines that whirr into motion with a life of their own.

This instalment of the documentary series Portraits of Another Life captures Gould searching for objects to repurpose and working in his studio as he explains his creative process and the evolution of his work over the years, including his more political recent pieces. Through animations as well as interviews with Gould’s father, a fellow artist, the video makes a strong case for keeping childhood fascinations alive. Gould’s art, too, serves as a reminder that much of the joy in making things lies in the physical, hands-on experience of it, rather than just the final result.

item.title: What life in Denmark shows about the power of emotional safety
item.dc:creator: Ruth Aharoni Nielsen
item.description:
A deep sense of ease – what the Danes call ‘tryg’ – is a collective responsibility that allows individuals to flourish

- by Ruth Aharoni Nielsen

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
For newcomers to Denmark, many things don’t always make sense. Parents leave sleeping babies outside cafés. Young children cycle to school alone. Primary schools don’t do homework, exams and competition. Success is quietly downplayed rather than celebrated. Meetings are spent revisiting the last meeting, planning the current one, eating together and preparing for the next meeting. Decisions are painfully slow, and everything is scheduled and regulated. Nothing is rushed. For me, and for many others who have made Denmark our home, much of everyday life initially seemed to defy the logic by which successful societies are supposed to function.

Marrying into Danish culture, and being a psychologist, I was intrigued by this, but had stopped worrying only when our eldest daughter reached junior high. Until then, I had to reluctantly trust the Danish line of reasoning that appears not only in schools, but across everyday life: you must first feel tryg.

What does it mean to feel tryg? The word is often translated as ‘safe’, but that is not quite right. It does not primarily refer to the absence of threat. Rather, it points to the presence of a particular state: the body at ease – calm, relaxed, with a sense of familiar warmth. Like the relaxed feeling of a child resting in her parents’ arms. In Danish, feeling tryg is not assumed to rise spontaneously. It is rather something that arises as a reaction to specific contexts that are deliberately cultivated. Members of the group implicitly take the responsibility to cultivate settings that promote and foster feeling tryg.

Certain conditions facilitate this emotional stance that allows us to be present, without scanning the environment or anticipating what might go wrong – or what might, suddenly, change. When feeling tryg, attention widens. The world can be met with a quiet, open curiosity. We take in what is happening around us and engage more easily and positively with others. We have the space to review the situation and be free to make the best decisions about what it requires of us.

In Danish culture, feeling tryg is not merely an inherent individual quality, it is rather a cultural and emotional concept that guides how the social world is designed. Predictable environments, well-known surroundings, consistent and trustworthy relationships, friendliness and pleasant spaces are all assumed to promote feeling tryghed – ‘safeness’ – for all.

When tryghed is absent, the body becomes more alert and more prepared. We begin to scan for what might go wrong, and uncertainty is harder to tolerate. We know this from ordinary moments: entering a new group and trying to read the room, sitting in a meeting or a classroom with unclear expectations, or speaking with someone whose tone is harsh or reactions unpredictable. Attention narrows, shifting away from what is being said and toward anticipating what might go wrong. On a basic level, the questions that preoccupy the mind are: friend or foe? Should I engage? Can I leave? Should I protect myself?

Danes extend tryghed everywhere: in classrooms, workplaces and public spaces

In line with decades of psychological research, the neuroscientist Stephen Porges has recently described how states of perceived safeness – a felt sense of being at ease – allow the nervous system to settle, making openness, joyful learning and social engagement possible. In this state of tryghed, tolerance and curiosity flourish, and so does prosocial behaviour. Unlike in traditional psychology, in Denmark, tryghed is not treated as a private matter. Creating environments that are tryg is seen as a shared responsibility and something that Danes take very seriously. This means that attention shifts from how individuals feel to how we structure shared conditions – and to how everyone feels. Physical and social settings are organised around this principle. Danes place a strong emphasis on cultivating environments that convey expectations very clearly – preferably in a friendly way. Actively fostering tryghed helps life feel pleasant and predictable enough for everyone to drop their guard. This is not just ‘safety’ in a physical sense, it’s a set of conditions that allows feelings of safeness to emerge in the group.

In Danish, these conditions are often referred to as ‘rammer’ or the ‘frameworks’ – in which tryghed for everyone is cultivated. Danes value tryghed and seek to extend it everywhere: in classrooms, workplaces and public spaces.

Certain rammer – certain conditions – allow tryghed to emerge. Over time, repeated experiences of feeling tryg accumulate into a form of implicit social knowledge: how to design the very conditions that make tryghed possible.

Cycling to work one morning, I passed an election poster. In large letters it read: Trygge mennesker tør – ‘People who feel tryg dare.’ The message was simple, almost self-evident. When we feel this deep safeness, we are free to engage, to innovate, to act, to move forward. It was not presented as a psychological insight, but as something one could assume people already understood – an election appeal to shared values and what does not need to be justified.

Once you start understanding tryghed in Denmark, it appears everywhere. In how classrooms are organised, in how school curricula are set, in how meetings are run, in how public spaces are designed. The same quiet premise: if people feel tryg, something else becomes possible.

Meetings and schedules are structured to reduce unnecessary uncertainty

In schools, the emphasis is not only on what children learn, but on designing physical and social environments in which they can learn. In family life, there is often a focus on maintaining pleasant and predictable structures and schedules. In neighbourhoods with many children, the streets are empty at 6 pm – everyone is at home having dinner.

In workplaces, meetings and schedules are structured to make expectations explicit and to reduce unnecessary uncertainty. Time is taken to align, to clarify, so that people know what is required of them. In public life, this orientation appears in small, taken-for-granted behaviours: people tend to follow shared rules, and actively maintain a sense of order that others can rely on. Dog poop is picked up, traffic rules are followed, common spaces are designed for safeness, and in turn are highly respected. Individuals intentionally maintain the conditions that foster safeness for everyone every day – and everything that ‘safeness for all’ brings with it. This commitment extends well beyond everyday interactions. It is reflected in the entitlements of society, from paid parental leave for both mothers and fathers to free healthcare and education, all designed to reduce unnecessary uncertainty across the life course.

None of this is absolute, it is not always consistent, and this commitment brings its tensions. For Danes, what is unfamiliar, unpredictable or new can easily be felt as unsettling. Decisions can be painfully lengthy, as more perspectives are considered and alignment is sought. Processes become careful, sometimes to the point of hesitation. Groups move toward consensus – because shared understanding is given high priority. It also affects how difference is experienced: ways of thinking or behaving that fall outside established patterns may feel less tryg, simply because they are unfamiliar. In this sense, tryghed does not only enable openness; it can also limit what is accepted or allowed to emerge.

Rules are designed to allow everyone to feel safeness – but they can make processes slower and heavier. The same conditions that create stability can make quick change more difficult. Over time, tolerance for messiness, ambiguity and rapid adjustment may be less practised, which can, in turn, affect resilience. Can a country that relies so heavily on tryghed be competitive in a rapidly changing world?

Stable relationships and trustworthy frameworks form an infrastructure that supports prosocial behaviour

As a tryg-driven society, Denmark is often described as stable and high-trust, yet it also performs remarkably well across measures such as innovation and economic performance. While liberal democracies are in decline, Denmark also consistently ranks high on the democracy index. Democracies are many things, but they depend heavily on systems of emotional regulation: when institutions and norms foster predictability and shared responsibility, trust and cooperation emerge; when they erode, suspicion and hostility take over.

One way to make sense of this is to shift the focus to everyday life. Stable relationships and trustworthy frameworks – designed to benefit all – form an infrastructure that supports prosocial behaviour. They paradoxically make learning and innovation less risky in an uncertain world.

Often in liberal democracies, political life is framed around concepts like ‘effectiveness’, ‘freedom’ or ‘equality’. In Denmark, the emphasis is more often placed on the felt experience of tryghed – and on whether everyday life promotes feeling safeness – through everyday acts of care performed by individuals and people in office alike. When safeness is not cultivated, a different logic takes hold: under conditions of uncertainty and threat, exclusion can begin to feel rational, and control preferable to openness and trust.

Last spring, I was standing with some of the ‘international’ parents on the grass, watching the annual school football match. These parents – like myself – had settled into life in Denmark, despite having other, sometimes more lucrative, options in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany or Canada. Among these parents there are CEOs of startup companies, heads of venture capital firms and high-profile consultants. We stood on the sidelines, watching our children run across the field, as one of the parents, Jeff, described something that had become difficult to explain to friends back home: how easy everyday life here felt.

Children cycling alone to school. Wallets returned. Streets kept clean. Systems that work. But also, something less visible – the sense that these conditions are not accidental. That someone, somewhere, has thought about how life should feel, and that this is a shared endeavour.

It is easy to notice the outcomes. It is harder to see the orientation behind them. Not only a commitment to rules or institutions, but to the ongoing work of maintaining conditions in which everyone can let their guard down. Perhaps this is what it means, in practice, to organise a society around care and tryghed – and why it may matter more than we tend to notice.

item.title: The social construction of emotions
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Are our emotions universal? How two landmark studies upended our view of emotions – and challenged colonial stereotypes

- Video by Then & Now

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Western imperialism was often justified as a moral imperative – colonising countries had a duty to civilise the ‘savages’ they encountered oceans away. This ‘white man’s burden’, as the English writer Rudyard Kipling called it, partially hinged on the notion that emotions are universal and biological, existing on a continuum between the refined rationality of Europeans and the uncontrolled emotionality of those they colonised.

In this video essay, the UK filmmaker Lewis Waller discusses two works of anthropology that challenged this paradigm: Never in Anger (1970), the US anthropologist Jean Briggs’s portrait of an Utku Inuit family, and Unnatural Emotions (1988), the US anthropologist Catherine Lutz’s account of emotions on Ifaluk Atoll in Micronesia. Placing these works in the context of the colonial past and more recent research, Waller makes the case that emotions aren’t biologically hardwired and universal, but filtered through sociocultural contexts and constantly being constructed.

item.title: Deciding to detransition
item.dc:creator: André Aram
item.description:
For two years, I lived as a trans woman – happy with my body, but fearful of the world it moved in

- by André Aram

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I was 19 when I first considered becoming a trans woman. I grew up in a household of women: my parents divorced when I was four, so it was just me, my mother and four sisters. ‘Deepen that voice!’ my uncles constantly reproached me. ‘You’re too delicate! Don’t walk like a girl!’ I’d realised from an early age that I was gay. In elementary school, there was a boy with whom I would hold hands in secret. One day we kissed; a teacher saw and scolded us. That’s when I began to understand this was wrong, though I didn’t know why.

My mother didn’t know how to deal with this. ‘I won’t accept a little faggot for a son,’ I heard her say countless times. She struggled with mental illness, including body dysmorphia, and rarely left the house; she thought people were laughing at her for being overweight. By the time I was eight, I was doing everything on my own – grocery shopping, going to the bank, taking the bus. During these errands, I’d sometimes stop at newsstands and admire the male bodies in magazines, fall in love with the princes in the cartoons.

Looking back, I realise that, for an effeminate, mixed-race, lower-middle-class boy on the outskirts of Brasília, there was always a predator lurking: a neighbour, a relative, someone with bad intentions. When I was 13, we started attending an evangelical church. There was no sense of belonging there either, for me; I was always seen as the guilty one. The pastor there would approach me and ask if I was homosexual.

‘The devil is preparing you for this,’ he warned. ‘You have to pray and fast.’

Once, I was at the home of a pastor who lived next to the church. We were counting flyers that would be distributed before a religious event. Night had fallen. The pastor went to the bathroom and returned in his underwear. Realising his intentions, I fled without saying a word. I left the church after that. That’s when I started spending time around the trans women in Brasília.

I would hang out with them in the industrial zone in Taguatinga, near the Coca-Cola factory, and in the red-light districts in the central parts of the city. Theirs was a world full of contradictions. They lived in houses owned by pimps, to whom they paid a daily fee to live on the properties and work in the streets. There was loud laughter and there was loud makeup – everything felt like a party. There were big egos and intense competition over looks, but food and wigs were freely shared. Once, when a trans woman returned home beaten by a client, the others came together to pay for her food, medicine and her share of the fee owed to the pimp.

By the time I was 16, I’d left home to live with a boyfriend. He was 16, too. Where we lived, in the gay ghettos, there were a lot of fights. But no one messed with me because they knew the trans women would defend me. When you’re young, you’re always looking for a sense of belonging you didn’t find in your own family. I found it in the trans women who accepted and welcomed me.

Some people experience body dysphoria from a very early age – what they see physically isn’t what they actually feel. For others, the possibility of being trans arises only later in life, when they can choose to be something other than who or what they are. I belong to the latter category: it was only after years of living alongside trans women that I began to realise I could be one, too.

My first attempt at transitioning was short-lived – three months into taking hormones, I stopped. My decision had less to do with my gender identity than the ways in which I thought changing it would foreclose possibilities for me. Simply put, I did not want to become a sex worker – often the only means of income for the trans women around me. It is a profession accompanied by a great deal of violence and psychological trauma; most trans women I knew used drugs to cope with that life. I liked their world, I liked being with them, but I didn’t like the situations they found themselves in.

Ten years later, after much reflection, I decided once more to transition. This time, I resolved to follow all the steps to fully become a woman. I began psychological counselling, then hormones under medical supervision. I’d already set aside the funds I’d need, through years of working at a beauty salon in an upper-middle-class neighbourhood in Brasília, a place specialising in hair extensions. The clients there were supportive, even if some found it strange. Some gave me earrings, makeup, clothes, even lingerie. Others asked whether I would now turn to sex work.

Within months, my body began to change. I was also studying nursing at the local university and when I returned for the second semester, I looked like a different person. When I got my breast implants, I was euphoric – I felt I would be a woman only after getting implants and wearing a dress. The other students complimented me, peppering me with questions. Some teachers ignored me; one insisted on calling me by my dead name. She’d never liked me, actually.

My social life changed drastically. People stop inviting you to birthdays and barbecues

As my body changed, I felt both fear and joy. My mother cried when she saw my breasts. I think they were tears of frustration but that didn’t bother me. I don’t think my mother ever stopped loving me – she worried only about the prejudice I would face. My sisters were happy that I was happy. I was happy: I was building a whole new self.

Maintaining a feminine appearance is expensive. Your hair has to be silky, straight and long, nails manicured, makeup flawless, clothes beautiful – not to mention the laser hair removal, hormone treatments and plastic surgeries. In order to ‘pass’ – that is, look more feminine so that society would be more accepting – I must have spent more than $25,000. Then, there are expenses you wouldn’t think to account for: occasionally, in order to avoid harassment, you can’t take the bus and you have to take a taxi. You even have to choose where you live carefully.

Despite all these efforts, my social life changed drastically. People stop inviting you to birthdays and barbecues – one friend told me she didn’t invite me because her relatives were evangelicals. She said she wanted to protect me from the possibility of being offended by them. Some began watching my every move, suspicious I would flirt with their boyfriends. It’s as if you’re no longer trustworthy; everything suddenly revolves around sexuality. Once, my friend and I were pelted with eggs on the street. Another time, I was at a nightclub and kissed a guy. Then a girl told him I was trans. He said he was going to the bathroom and would be back. I never saw him again.

After two years of living as a trans woman, I decided to reverse my transition. The truth is, there wasn’t a single day I wasn’t afraid for my life. For many people, gender transition is a vital necessity, but for me it wasn’t. It was a choice I’d made, and I’d made it happily, but it came with costs: the constant shadow of violence, estranged and murdered friends, the high price of upkeep.

I began to wonder whether it was worth going through all that just to be a woman.

For 18 consecutive years, Brazil has topped the global list of countries with the highest number of murders of trans people. Last year, there were 80 documented homicides of trans people. We wake up prepared for war every day. One friend – we called her ‘little whore’ because she was all of five feet tall, 22 years old and sweet – was seen on the street getting into a client’s car, but she never returned. We know she was murdered, but we don’t know how or why. Another, Paula Maia, became a quadriplegic after an attempt on her life, but what ultimately killed her was the industrial silicone she’d used to modify her body – a primitive, painful and irreversible procedure. Another named Julia died after being attacked by an older man who lived in the red-light districts; he would go out with some of the sex workers but had a habit of humiliating trans women: ‘You’re ugly, you’re fat, you’re not worth what you charge.’ Julia argued back once, so he stabbed her.

Life as a trans woman is far riskier than as a gay man

Nothing happened to him. I see him on the street sometimes because he lives near my salon.

I sought counselling for a while and began to ask myself: Why can’t I go back? Little by little, I began telling people about my decision. Some tried to dissuade me, others chastised me for being indecisive, while others, such as my evangelical family, readily supported me – to them, it was a sign of ‘liberation’. Almost everyone understood, however, that life as a trans woman is far riskier than as a gay man.

Some asked if I had become evangelical. This is common in Brazil, where the evangelical population is booming: people who detransitioned after converting, fed false promises that everything would be different for them after, or those who’d fallen into drug use or become homeless and were offered support only on the condition that they stop being trans. I’ve seen how that goes. For many people, religion is a pretext to gain social acceptance because it’s extremely difficult to deconstruct something you’ve built and suddenly declare: ‘I don’t want this anymore and I’m going to change.’ Not everyone has that courage.

I began saving up once more, this time to pay for the removal of my breast implants. If it’s expensive to become a trans woman, it’s also not cheap to stop being one. I’ve heard from others who would like to consider doing so but lack the money or job prospects to do so. A woman named Aline who lived in southern Brazil reached out to me at the time, saying she too wanted to detransition. But it was difficult for her as she’d already altered her jaw, nose and forehead.

It’s been 10 years since I stopped identifying as a trans woman. I was happy with my trans body, and I’m happy now too. It was an experience I wanted to have, and it changed my outlook on life. Trans life in Brazil can be very cruel, but it also offers a sense of belonging. It was important for me to have had that. When you actually live through it, you realise the price is high – some are willing to pay it, while others are not. Those who criticise me don’t understand this is my existence, my decision, and every human is unique.

item.title: How mental disorders play havoc with our motivation
item.dc:creator: Matthias Pillny
item.description:
Feeling energised to do something depends on a cost-benefit analysis that psychiatric conditions scramble in different ways

- by Matthias Pillny

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
There are days when even little things seem surprisingly difficult. Replying to a message. Taking a shower. Going shopping. Calling a friend back. These are small, everyday actions, often done in a few minutes. And yet, for many people, these sometimes feel like tasks for which they have barely enough energy.

When we see this kind of struggle in a friend or relative, or feel it in ourselves, simple explanations might come to mind: a lack of drive; a need for meaningful goals; laziness. You just need to pull yourself together. You know it would do you good.

This view overlooks something important. Between considering or intending to do something and actually doing it, there is a psychological process that usually remains invisible in everyday life. Colloquially, people call this process ‘motivation’. But motivation is not like an internal fuel tank that is full or empty. Rather, it involves a continually running cost-benefit calculation.

Our brains constantly analyse the extent to which an action is worth the effort, which informs us about the seemingly best option at any given moment. This process is called effort-based decision-making. Since the workings of this process are usually hidden, it’s easy to make wrong inferences about the reasons for a person’s choices or inactivity.

However, scientists have devised ways to observe this process in action, allowing us to learn more about what’s happening when a person weighs doing or not doing something. Understanding this process encourages more helpful attitudes toward those who struggle with everyday motivation, which is often connected to a broader mental health condition. It can also inform the best ways to help someone overcome their challenges.

The analysis of costs and benefits usually takes place so quickly that we barely notice it. Should I answer this email now or put it off until later? Should I exercise after work or rest on the sofa? Should I meet my friends tonight even though I’m already tired? To answer these questions, our brains (and, actually, the brains of all vertebrates) weigh three things against each other. How effortful will it be for me to achieve this goal? How rewarding will it be for me – enough to outweigh the costs? And how likely is it that the reward will actually occur?

Most of the time, this process is very helpful. It prevents us from becoming completely exhausted, from being constantly disappointed, or from wasting our time and effort. But the cost-benefit analysis can also go wrong. From the outside, this can look like laziness or indifference, and it often results in difficulties managing work or school activities, relationships or self-care routines.

Altered cost-benefit calculations seem particularly relevant in the context of conditions such as depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. In people diagnosed with these disorders, motivational difficulties are common. While other symptoms of these disorders might be better known – eg, sad mood in depression, mood swings in bipolar disorder, or delusions and hallucinations in schizophrenia – motivational problems commonly pose the strongest long-term barrier to wellbeing. They often persist beyond the acute phases of the illness and are currently considered difficult to treat. As a result, they can have a lasting impact on daily life. When someone struggles to take the necessary steps to keep up with a friend, go to appointments or apply for a job, for example, it can lead to a downward spiral in terms of social participation, wellbeing or professional opportunities. These experiences often prompt negative self-evaluations (such as: I’m a complete failure), which can further exacerbate someone’s motivational problems.

The internal cost-benefit calculation seemed to have become unbalanced in people with these disorders

The concept of effort-based decision-making allows researchers to look behind the scenes and better understand the mechanisms underlying these motivational problems at the moment of choice. To do this, researchers use computer-based tasks that are designed to isolate the decision-making process as precisely as possible.

In a typical study, a person has to choose between an easier task and a more difficult one. The easy task might consist of pressing a button 30 times with the index finger of the dominant hand in order to receive a small reward, such as one dollar. The difficult task might involve pressing a button 100 times with the little finger of the non-dominant hand, but receiving a larger reward in return. Across repeated trials, the size of the reward for the difficult task changes. In some versions, the probability of receiving the reward also changes: one might have, for example, a 12 per cent, 50 per cent or 88 per cent chance of receiving the reward for a task. Sometimes even the amount of effort required for a given reward varies. Before each decision, participants see how much effort is required for a task, what reward is possible and how likely it is that they will receive this reward. Then they decide what to do. The outcome of interest is when someone decides that the more difficult task is worth it.

In a recent meta-analysis, my colleagues and I summarised the results of 68 studies on effort-based decision-making in mental disorders. We found a clear pattern showing that people with schizophrenia, depression or bipolar disorder were less likely than people without these diagnoses to choose effortful actions in order to obtain a reward. This reduction was most pronounced in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and smaller, but still statistically significant, in depression.

Typically, when a reward becomes larger or more likely to be attained, people invest more effort. It seems more worthwhile. In clinical groups, however, this adjustment was weakened. People with schizophrenia, depression or bipolar disorder did not increase their effort to the same extent as others when rewards became larger or more certain. Their internal cost-benefit calculation seemed to have become unbalanced.

At first glance, this speaks to a common motivational problem across different diagnoses. However, the story gets even more interesting when we examine why this happens.

One way to approach this question is through computational modelling. In this statistical method, a computer model is used to try to reproduce a person’s decisions by testing different explanations for their behaviour. Let us imagine several people who rarely choose the more difficult task over the easier one. One person may avoid the task because the effort feels particularly burdensome to them. Another may avoid it because the reward has little motivating force for them. A third person might primarily have difficulty bringing all the information together and translating it into an informed decision. Computer-based models help researchers distinguish between these possibilities, which is important for understanding where the cost-benefit calculation goes wrong.

Our review of computational modelling studies suggests that the motivational problems in different mental disorders arise in partly different ways. For people with schizophrenia, the results often indicate that amounts of effort, reward and probability of receiving the reward are all less influential for decision-making. The difficulty seems to lie in integrating and processing multiple pieces of information in a situation and making them usable for one’s own decisions. This fits with the findings of our meta-analysis, according to which cognitive difficulties – in working memory or processing speed, for example – are associated with alterations in effort-based decision-making in schizophrenia.

A person experiencing mania might work through several nights, the effort not feeling burdensome at all

When it is difficult for someone to keep relevant information in mind, update it and compare it with other information, then decision-making becomes more difficult. For example, if someone with schizophrenia wants to return to work and needs to decide whether to apply for a particular job, even taking the first step requires weighing several bits of information: the effort involved in starting an application or making a phone call, the potential benefits of applying and the likelihood that they will get a job offer. If all the relevant information can’t be readily integrated into a cost-benefit calculation, this might feel overwhelming. Instead the person may choose less demanding options or postpone taking action.

In depression, the picture looks somewhat different. Here, studies using computational modelling often suggest that effort carries special weight. The reward may still be attractive, but the path to it feels too effortful to seem worthwhile. A person may know that it could do them good to meet up with a friend, for instance. Perhaps they even expect that they will experience some pleasure from it. And yet getting dressed, leaving the house, getting there and having a conversation might feel like daunting obstacles.

In bipolar disorder, the evidence base is more limited. The current illness state probably plays an important role. In more stable phases, people with bipolar disorder may still be able to weigh effort, reward and probability relatively well. In depressive phases, their pattern resembles that seen in depression, with effort being experienced as particularly burdensome. In manic or hypomanic phases of the disorder, the problem could manifest in a dysregulated willingness to exert effort in situations where reward and probability are actually low. For example, a person experiencing mania might work through several nights on a business plan and sell various belongings to invest in the plan because, to them, the potential reward seems extremely high, and the effort does not feel burdensome at all.

These differences suggest that there is not one solution for all motivational problems. For some people, it may be helpful to make rewards more concrete, more immediate and more emotionally tangible. For example, ‘Seeing friends is good for me’ might become: ‘After 10 minutes of conversation, I usually feel a little less alone.’ For others, the critical change might be to reduce the felt costs of an action, such as by breaking down a task into smaller steps. Still others may need support with planning, or with comparing effort and reward more clearly and meaningfully.

Some existing therapeutic approaches use techniques that may act on these mechanisms. Positive affect treatment focuses on helping people look forward to rewarding experiences and engage more fully with positive events. Cognitive behavioural social skills training includes problem-solving modules that involve dividing planned activities into smaller steps. Cognitive remediation programmes aim to strengthen abilities such as attention and memory, which are needed to weigh effort against possible rewards. The next step is to bring together methods like these into a more comprehensive treatment that addresses the specific reasons why activities feel unrewarding or difficult, and that can be tailored to each person’s needs.

Sometimes, inactivity is the visible result of an invisible calculation that has become unbalanced

The effort-based decision-making lens can also inform how we respond to motivational problems in ourselves and others. Things like ‘You just have to start’ or ‘Once you do it, you’ll feel better’ can be frustrating to hear because they imply that the problem is simply a lack of willpower. A curious, empathic attitude is likely to be more helpful. What exactly feels difficult? Is the effort too great? Is the reward too far away? Is the outcome too uncertain? Is the task too complex to plan? Such questions are more helpful than just telling someone to make an effort or pointing out that it will be worth it in the end.

Motivation is not a fixed character trait, but a dynamic process, one that changes with mood, context, cognition, symptoms, exhaustion, social support and expectations. This insight is not relevant only for people with mental disorders. Everyone has moments when the internal calculation tilts one way or the other. Consequently, the email stays unread, the sports shoes sit by the door or the call from a friend goes unanswered. When in doubt, we might accuse ourselves of being weak or undisciplined. But perhaps it’s really that the reward is not clear enough, the task seems too effortful or the prospect of success feels too doubtful. Sometimes, inactivity is the visible result of an invisible calculation that has become unbalanced. This is a problem that calls for attention rather than criticism.

item.title: Chu Prayad
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Power, precision and acrobatic high kicks – the Southeast Asian sport of sepak takraw offers Prayad relief from the road

- Directed by Habib Yazdi and Joseph Marra

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The Southeast Asian sport of sepak takraw is a hybrid of football and volleyball in which two teams separated by a net score points by grounding a ball in their opponents’ territory without using their hands. And, as this short documentary captures, when played at a high level it’s thrilling to watch, requiring balance, precision, cooperation and acrobatic high kicks from its players. The film offers a brief window into the life of a young man named Prayad, who juggles his often stressful work as a taxi driver on the streets of Bangkok, Thailand with hard-fought sepak takraw matches among friends. In the game, he finds facets of life many people lose as they become adults burdened by responsibilities – play, exercise and camaraderie.

Via Labocine

item.title: How to handle jealous feelings
item.dc:creator: Carla Marie Manly
item.description:
Jealousy can be a useful, insightful emotion – if you manage it well. Get curious about your jealousy to get a grip on it

- by Carla Marie Manly

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Jealousy can rear its head in many ways. Have you ever felt displeased and resentful that a partner showed someone else ‘too much’ attention? Or that they spoke fondly about an ex? Or maybe you’ve felt unsettled when a best friend or a family member made social plans that didn’t include you? In situations like these, your feelings of jealousy might gnaw at you under the surface, or you could feel so hurt that you lash out at someone you love.

Jealousy is a normal emotion and, like other emotions, it can affect people in both healthy and unhealthy ways. At its worst, jealousy can keep you stuck in negativity, anger and resentment. But when it’s managed well, jealousy can be useful – an alert that you are feeling threatened in some way. There’s a lot to unravel when it comes to this commonly misunderstood emotion. And the more you learn how to gain insight from jealous feelings, the less likely you’ll be to cause yourself or others unnecessary angst or pain.

This Guide is for anyone who wants to know more about jealousy, though it could be particularly helpful for those who chronically struggle to understand or respond well to jealous feelings. The goal, in any case, isn’t to eradicate jealousy, but to learn to engage with it in beneficial ways.

What is jealousy?

Jealousy arises when the love, affection or attention you receive from someone else seems to be at risk, usually because you perceive the actions or presence of another person as competition. Although ‘jealousy’ and ‘envy’ are often used synonymously, envy involves wanting something that another person has, whereas jealousy generally points to a lack of security in a relationship. In short, feelings of jealousy are triggered by a sense of relational danger. This danger might be real or imagined; the mind often doesn’t differentiate between the two.

When jealous feelings come up in response to an actual event – such as when a romantic partner admits to infidelity – it is what clinical psychologists call reactive jealousy. As a therapist, I have worked with many people whose jealousy stemmed from concrete experiences like this. One client’s jealousy arose, for example, when they discovered that their loved one had been communicating with an ‘old flame’ on social media. Although the situation hadn’t escalated to physical infidelity, the partner who discovered it felt hurt and betrayed. In this case, the jealous feelings were an emotional alarm bell – an indicator of a potential threat to the relationship.

Suspicious jealousy is different from reactive jealousy: it stems from personal insecurities rather than a concrete event. In a romantic context, for example, suspicious jealousy can arise even when a partner has never shown any evidence of being unfaithful. If you tend to feel jealous about someone even though they are open and honest with you, you might be struggling with suspicious jealousy.

In my work with couples in therapy, I’ve noticed that suspicious jealousy is often an indicator of difficulties with relating to others, which are rooted in one’s past. For example, I recently worked with a couple where one partner’s attachment style led them to feel chronically insecure in the relationship and overly dependent on the other partner. Although both partners were faithful and committed to the relationship, unresolved wounds from childhood often left this partner feeling deeply anxious and jealous. When underlying issues like these are at work, the path to improvement involves diving into those unhealed wounds from the past to develop healthy awareness and responses in the present.

When jealousy is chronic and unprocessed, it can hurt self-esteem, increase stress, and create further difficulties in relationships. I’ve seen ongoing jealousy cause serious harm in friendships, family relationships and romantic partnerships. In one case, a long-term friendship was irrevocably damaged when one person became so jealous about her friend’s blossoming romance that she actively tried to derail it. It became clear that the jealous friend – who struggled with anxiety and low self-esteem – felt threatened by her friend’s delight-filled new relationship. In the same way, unresolved jealousy between family members (for example, chronically vying for parents’ attention, validation and other resources) or between romantic partners can eat away at relationships.

Whatever the source of your jealousy, if it’s something that you struggle with, you can learn how to process and respond to jealous feelings differently, so that when you do experience them, you feel more regulated and empowered. The process of managing jealousy can take some time (especially if it’s an ongoing issue), but you can create real changes, starting now, by increasing your self-awareness and practising mindful emotional regulation. Next, I’ll share some ways to do that.

item.title: What is hidden in the photographs we keep of each other?
item.dc:creator: Sawa Kurotani
item.description:
Returning to family photo albums in my mother’s apartment in Japan, I was struck by the stories the images didn’t tell

- by Sawa Kurotani

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Alone in the cluttered spare bedroom of my mother’s apartment in Japan, I found myself surrounded by the accumulated contents of our family’s life. There were towers of boxes, and stacks of books, piles of old clothes and miscellaneous household items – the residue of decades that no one had been able to sort through. My sister had died unexpectedly years earlier; my father, too, was gone. So I had flown back to Japan from the United States to help my mother, who had been hospitalised after breaking her hip and had also begun a slow descent into dementia. In the apartment, I spotted a moving box with the words ‘Sawa’s Albums’ written on the outside. When I recognised my mother’s handwriting, I broke down in tears.

Inside the box were hundreds of photographs of my sister and me. They were the product of my parents’ sustained and deliberate labour, beginning in the mid-1960s, when taking pictures still required skill and expense. My father, an avid amateur photographer, kept a meticulous visual record of our growth, which my mother arranged into 14 neatly organised and captioned albums.

These albums depict the family life my parents worked hard to build: my sister and me on the beach with packed bento lunches, standing stiffly in our new clothes in front of our old house on the first day of school, and smiling on the steps of a Shinto shrine on New Year’s Day. As children, we would pull out the albums time and again, telling and retelling to ourselves the stories of our family.

Now, decades later, I flipped through our childhood albums alone. Black-and-white photographs gave way to faded colour prints. In the early years, they were accompanied by my mother’s delicate handwriting, naming dates and places; later, her captions were replaced by my childish writing, then by my cheeky teenage annotations. I immersed myself in the faces and stories I remembered from childhood.

At first, the experience felt like a return to something intimately familiar. Gradually, something else emerged. Something harder to name. As I turned the pages, I felt faint but persistent prickles of unease. I wanted to understand where that unease came from.

The first thing I noticed was who appeared in these photographs – and, later, who did not. In my first year, I was often pictured with my mother. But she appeared mostly as an ever-present caretaker at the periphery: photographs showed her hands steadying me from behind or her skirt at the edge of the frame. My mother’s presence lessened over the next few years, and I was increasingly captured in action – walking, running, playing or climbing trees – by myself or with my childhood friends. My sister was born when I was four and, from that point, photographs showed the two of us together. Throughout these years, my father largely remained behind the camera, except in a few snapshots taken by family friends.

Then I began to wonder: where were the pictures of all four of us together? I went through the albums in the box once more and found none.

Even the structure of the albums reflected a certain separation – each of us had our own and there was no shared family album

There were almost no images of my parents as a married couple, either. I searched the apartment and found a separate collection of my parents’ photographs. Aside from their wedding portraits and a small number of snapshots from their courtship, I found no anniversary pictures, no photos of them from vacation trips or family events. There were no images of them sharing a quiet moment at home. In fact, there was almost no visual record of their togetherness.

Even the structure of the albums reflected a certain separation – each of us had our own, individually named, and there was no shared ‘family album’. When my sister and I were very young, my mother decided which prints went into our separate albums. Once we were old enough, she would let us divide them ourselves. Each album became an individual record of childhood, which also stood in as the shared record of our family history.

Taken together, these absences formed a pattern, made all the more striking by the care and detail that went into documenting our lives. So much had been preserved – outings, milestones, gestures, occasions – that what was omitted became harder to dismiss.

Only later did I recognise that I had begun what the cultural theorist Annette Kuhn calls ‘memory work’: returning to photographs to look carefully at what they show and, just as importantly, at what they do not. ‘A photograph,’ Susan Sontag explains in On Photography (1977), ‘is not only an image (as a painting is an image), an interpretation of the real; it is also a trace, something directly stencilled off the real, like a footprint or a death mask.’ Photos record not merely how things looked, but the fact that they existed at all. Family photographs in particular present themselves as visual testimony of lived experience.

But they can also do more than that – sometimes photographs participate in the construction of our memories by making certain relationships and sentiments visible while leaving others in shadow. As I looked into those shadows, the old feelings, which I believed I had long since left behind, came back to me: resentment at my father’s need for control, empathy and frustration toward my mother’s resignation, and the vague but persistent loneliness and fear of abandonment I had carried through childhood.

Our parents’ affection could seem present at one moment and unreachable the next

As I sat with these emotions, my thoughts turned to the deprivations of my parents’ own childhoods. My parents grew up in Tokyo and Yokohama during and immediately after the Second World War. Their family homes, along with most of their possessions, were destroyed during the firebombings in 1945. They came of age in conditions of material scarcity, in households shaped by loss and disruption. There are very few photographs of their early lives; survival left little room for documentation.

By the time they reached adulthood, they faced a different world of expectations. In the postwar period, during the decades of rapid economic growth in Japan, a new middle-class ideal took hold that centred on the nuclear family. Together, my parents built their lives around that ideal. My father became a breadwinner, working long hours outside the home. My mother became a full-time homemaker, responsible for managing the household and raising the children. Photographs of their thriving daughters became a record of their achievement.

My sister and I accepted the family story the albums told when we were young children. By the time we were in our late teens, we had begun to see another side of that story. Sitting at the kitchen table late at night, we often returned to the same insecurity we had held since childhood.
