We knew that our parents had given us a stable home, a good education, family outings and vacations. At the same time, we couldn’t always feel emotional closeness. Our parents’ affection could seem present at one moment and unreachable the next, and we learned, each in our own way, not to count on it. It seemed as though some forms of intimacy did not have a place in the family my parents knew how to build.

Marianne Hirsch’s concept of ‘postmemory’ helped me name this inheritance. She describes how the pain or trauma of one generation can reverberate through the lives of the next, even when they haven’t witnessed or experienced the cause. My parents’ childhood years, shaped by war and scarcity, were not memories my sister and I carried. Yet they shaped the family life my parents made for us and the emotional atmosphere in which we grew up.

The abundance and absences in our photo albums tell a layered story of a family built in the aftermath of loss. The photographs preserve the visible signs of recovery – the ordinary pleasures and routines of a stable middle-class family life. But the silences point to what remained harder to repair: things like intimacy and emotional assurance. I knew they cared for me. What puzzled me was whether affection could be felt and depended on between parents and children or between husband and wife, within a family.

What moments are consistently recorded, and which seem to leave no trace?

As an anthropologist, I also see the unmistakable remnants of the older model of the Japanese household in my family photographs. In this model, known as ie, the family functioned less as a site of emotional intimacy than as a unit organised around roles and continuity. Seen through this lens, my parents’ positions – in photographs and life – become more nuanced. My father’s absence from the frame signals distance, but it also reflects his dedication to what he considered his role as head of the household. My mother’s partial or peripheral presence in the images mirrored a life structured around the gendered role of service and support. It was also the visible trace of care that made the rest of us photographable.

These forms of care, however real, did not always become emotionally legible while we were growing up. After my sister died, I carried anger toward my parents that I could not fully explain. Only now, returning to these photographs from this new vantage point, do I begin to see that the anger reached back to something older – the uncertainty my sister and I shared about whether our parents’ affection would be there when we most needed it. I also understand, finally, how hard my parents tried to give us a better start in life than the one they had been given. If they fell short in offering emotional security, I can now see this as something more than failure. It is part of what they had inherited from their own childhoods.

This is what learning to practise ‘memory work’, learning to look carefully at what is or isn’t captured by photographs, has given me: a way to hold together truths about our family that once felt impossible to reconcile. My parents’ real care and emotional distance, the yearnings they pursued and the sacrifices they made, the uncertainty my sister and I shared, my youthful disappointments, and my renewed gratitude for the safe and stable childhood I was given – they are all real, and all deeply human.

For readers who have family photographs of their own, whether preserved in albums or stored on phones, it’s worth asking this: what is difficult to see in those images? Which people are photographed together and which are not? Which relationships appear only indirectly through traces at the edge of the frame? What moments are consistently recorded, and which seem to leave no trace? And how might your own memories – what you felt but could not have named at the time – change the way you observe those images now?

Asking these questions is a way of seeing the photographic records of our lives more carefully. It’s a way of recognising that their silences, as much as their contents, can carry meaning.

item.title: Black men suffer racial trauma yet are seen as the threat
item.dc:creator: Yamonte Cooper
item.description:
The very conditions that subject Black men to chronic strain make it hard for them to receive the help they need and deserve

- by Yamonte Cooper

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In my clinical and research work, I have heard versions of the same story many times. A Black man comes into the therapy room saying he is sleeping poorly. He feels irritable. He has started withdrawing from people he cares about because he does not want to keep explaining why ordinary situations leave him so tense.

At first, it sounds a lot like everyday stress. But then he goes on to describe a supervisor who repeatedly questions his competence, coworkers who describe his tone as aggressive when he speaks directly, or a store employee who follows him aisle by aisle. He may mention being stopped by police years earlier, watching another Black man’s death replayed online, or worrying that his son will one day have to learn the same rules of self-protection.

Many clinicians might still hear general anxiety, anger, depression, guardedness or poor engagement. Those words may describe part of what is visible. But I believe that this misses the serious chronic injury underneath. What looks like emotional shutdown is often a survival strategy. What looks like anger is often the surface of grief, shame or exhaustion. And what looks like mistrust may be an accurate memory of institutions that have not been safe. In other words, the man’s feelings and behaviours (and those of many other Black men like him) are an understandable response to racial trauma.

Society has become increasingly comfortable talking about trauma. The term now appears everywhere, applied to experiences ranging from acute violence to everyday stress. This expanded attention has brought greater awareness to suffering that was once ignored, which is welcome. But I’m conscious that it has also led to concerns: if everything is trauma, does the concept lose its meaning?

I understand these reservations. Not every painful or unjust experience is traumatic. But I’m not arguing that all experiences of racism qualify as trauma. Mine is a narrower claim: that sustained exposure to racialised threat, dehumanisation and constraint across multiple domains of life can produce a form of chronic psychological injury that remains widely misrecognised, particularly in Black men.

Any discussion of racial trauma must acknowledge that Black women also experience profound and persistent racial harm. My focus on Black men is not an attempt to rank suffering. Instead, my aim is to draw attention to the specific pattern of exposure and misrecognition that affects Black men. Harmful stereotypes about Blackness are not gender-neutral. They are often organised through Black maleness, especially through associations with threat, danger, criminality and aggression. This means that Black male distress can be misread not only because it is racialised, but because it is interpreted through stereotypes that already cast Black men as dangerous or difficult to manage.

Black men are exposed to a gendered form of anti-Blackness that marks them as threatening, punishable and economically disposable

In a 2020 Gallup survey, Black men in the US were more than twice as likely as Black women to say that people acted afraid of them (27 per cent, compared with 11 per cent) and were also more likely to report being treated with less courtesy and viewed as dishonest. National mortality research estimates that Black men and boys face about a one in 1,000 lifetime risk of being killed by police, roughly 2.5 times the risk for white men and boys. Economic data show a different but related pattern: in their 2019 study of nearly the entire US population, the Harvard economist Raj Chetty and colleagues show that the Black/white income gap, after accounting for parental income, was driven by differences in wages and employment among Black men, and Black boys had lower incomes in adulthood than white boys in 99 per cent of Census tracts.

Taken together, these and other findings suggest that Black men are not only exposed to anti-Black racism in general; they are exposed to a gendered form of anti-Blackness that marks them as threatening, punishable and economically disposable. Unlike the kind of distressing and harmful events that are traditionally associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), these constraints on Black men are not about any single event; they are structural and persistent. These conditions create a chronic threatening environment, where control over that threat is limited, and exposure to it is ongoing.

This constant exposure to threat produces a distinct kind of chronic psychological strain rather than a single episodic shock. Black men respond understandably with vigilance, guardedness, anger, emotional withdrawal or exhaustion.

Yet wider society mostly fails to recognise Black men’s experiences as racial trauma. And it rarely reads Black men’s behaviours as a necessary coping response.

Black men can be perceived more negatively than other race/gender groups on several stereotype dimensions. In their study of gendered racial stereotypes, the Princeton political scientists Corrine McConnaughy and Ismail White found that white respondents were especially likely to view Black men as violent and promiscuous, and least likely to view them as nurturing. These perceptions operate quickly and often outside conscious awareness, shaping attention, interpretation and response. This is not simply a matter of prejudice or dislike. It involves a culturally conditioned fear response that shapes how Black men are perceived and treated across contexts. Many people experience this fear as automatic and self-protective, which makes them less likely to question it.

This misrecognition has particular consequences. Anti-Black misandry affects how Black male emotion is interpreted across ordinary and institutional settings. A Black man’s guardedness may be read as hostility. His anger may be read as danger rather than as a response to repeated violation. His mistrust may be treated as paranoia or noncompliance rather than as a memory of institutions that have not been safe. In clinical settings, these readings can shape diagnosis and treatment. Hypervigilance, irritability, emotional shutdown or reluctance to disclose may be interpreted as aggression, oppositionality, poor engagement or pathology rather than as adaptations to chronic racial stress. The injury is compounded when trauma responses are interpreted through stereotypes that make Black men appear threatening rather than injured, difficult to manage rather than wounded.

By the time he enters therapy, he may already have learned to monitor his voice, posture, facial expression and emotional range

The result is a paradox: the very conditions that produce injury also make that injury difficult for clinicians and wider society to recognise. Black men express their distress in ways that are easily misinterpreted, and therefore more likely to be managed as a problem than understood as a response to harm. The effect is cumulative. Distress is repeatedly misrecognised as threat. Coping strategies are repeatedly interpreted as pathology.

As a result, a Black man may have to make his suffering appear calm, reasonable and nonthreatening before it can be recognised as suffering at all.

Consider the man I described in my opening vignette. By the time he enters therapy, he may already have learned to monitor his voice, posture, facial expression and emotional range. At work, he may know that directness can be called aggression. In public, he may know that ordinary movement can attract suspicion. In medical or mental health settings, he may know that mistrust can be treated as pathology rather than as a response to institutions that have historically failed Black people. None of these moments alone has to explain everything. Over time, their cumulative effect can be more profound than any single incident might suggest.

Importantly, these dynamics – between the threats faced by Black men and their coping responses – are not well explained by appeals to masculinity norms. Black men themselves do not primarily describe their experiences in terms of performing masculinity. Instead, their concerns often reflect something more basic: a claim to dignity, to safety, and to full recognition as human beings. In this sense, the issue is not masculinity, but manhood in a humanistic and existential sense. It is about the conditions under which a person is allowed to exist without being treated as a threat.

Although the dynamics affecting Black men are especially pronounced in the United States, similar patterns of racialised threat perception and differential treatment can be observed in other contexts, making this both a national and a broader social phenomenon. For instance, young Black men in the UK’s capital were 17 times more likely to be stopped and searched by the police compared with the general population, according to analysis by the security and crime scholar Matt Ashby at University College London in 2022; and the UK government’s Lammy Review in 2017 found that Black men were 41 per cent more likely than white men to receive a prison sentence for comparable drug offences at Crown Court.

I hope by drawing attention to the racial trauma experienced by many Black men, wider society will begin to change its interpretation of behaviours that too often are seen as problematic rather than as an understandable response to chronic threat. My hope is for vigilance to no longer be mistaken for paranoia. For anger to no longer be read solely as aggression. And for withdrawal to no longer be treated as disengagement.

For clinicians like me, this means shifting from asking ‘What is wrong with this person?’ to asking ‘What conditions might have made their response necessary?’

For others, it requires a similar shift in perception. Recognising racial trauma in Black men does not require you to become a clinician. It requires a different kind of attention in everyday life. When a Black man appears guarded, angry, quiet, mistrustful or withdrawn, the first question should not be what is wrong with him, but what has he had to carry, anticipate or survive. The task is to resist the reflex that turns Black male pain into threat, and to make room for that pain to be seen as pain.

Until racial trauma in Black men is seen clearly, psychology and society as a whole will continue to overlook a form of injury that is both pervasive and deeply consequential.

item.title: How to ignite your creativity
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Turn a mistake into art, write your own postcard: crafty ideas to escape the doom-scroll and jumpstart your creative practice

- Video by Struthless

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: Having a regular creative practice – music, writing, crafting, painting or whatever your preferred medium may be – has been shown to increase your overall sense of wellbeing. And, as the Australian artist and YouTube creator Campbell Walker (aka Struthless) discusses in this whimsical homespun video, in our era of infinite social feeds, making things has the added benefit of liberating you from the dreaded doom-scroll. Keeping in mind that, often, just getting started is the hardest part of creative work, Walker offers 10 crafty ideas – including ‘turn a mistake into art’ and ‘answer famous questions’ – to overcome the obstacles of fatigue, overwhelm, and perfectionism, and get the creative juices flowing.

item.title: Why moving on after a breakup makes you a better person
item.dc:creator: Matthew Barnfield
item.description:
They say time heals a broken heart. But do the hard work of moving on, and you do more than heal – you improve yourself

- by Matthew Barnfield

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘It is small use telling oneself “Stop being in love”,’ wrote Iris Murdoch in The Sovereignty of Good (1970). ‘Deliberately falling out of love is not a jump of the will.’ If you have ever suffered a romantic breakup, you will be familiar with the challenge of moving on. You cannot just decide to do it. It takes time. To quote a message I once received: ‘You’ll get there, and it hits you really suddenly, one day you’re like, wow what, I don’t care?’ All I had to do was wait.

Because moving on from a heartbreak requires such patience, it can seem like time itself is what does the work of healing you. Just as for a broken bone, time is the best healer for a broken heart. This is the passive view of moving on. Let time do its thing and all will be well.

But a broken bone, without a splint and support, will heal defectively. Likewise, if I remained passive, could I really expect to get better? After all, it is when a relationship is truly and permanently over that we need to move on. And what is permanent once remains permanent forever; time alone makes no difference to the permanence of loss. If all I could do was wait, would that be reassuring? I would have no agency, no way to shape the moved-on version of myself.

So perhaps it is preferable to think that moving on takes a while not because it is a passive process in which time itself heals all wounds, but for the opposite reason: it requires challenging, active work. As Murdoch put it:

What is needed is a reorientation which will provide an energy of a different kind, from a different source … Deliberately falling out of love … is the acquiring of new objects of attention and thus of new energies as a result of refocusing.

The question this active view of moving on raises is this: what is this work of acquiring new objects of attention, this different kind of energy, its different source? What is the activity of moving on?

When you’re in a relationship, all being well, you have what philosophers call a unified valuational perspective: you value your partner and your life together, and this value shapes your choices and actions in consistent ways. Take Joel and Clementine, who share this kind of love. Joel turns down the advances of attractive strangers on a night out. Clementine makes career choices that allow her to live in the same location as Joel. They don’t value these other things – freedom to date other people, career progress that eats up all their quality time together – in a way that inherently puts them in tension with valuing their relationship. In other words, valuing their relationship is compatible with the rest of their lives; it’s what the philosopher Valerie Tiberius calls an ‘appropriate’ value. When that changes, their relationship starts to strain, and it takes work, together, to put it right.

But if that work fails, maybe Clementine will break up with Joel. Then Joel’s valuational perspective fractures. Losing someone you love leaves you wanting them back. That value has become inappropriate. This creates a small part of you that recognises there might be value in no longer endorsing that value. It has to be that way: no one really thinks that being distraught is a good way to live the rest of their life. The trouble is that you can value only one of those things – to be back with your ex or no longer to need them – to the extent that you do not value the other.

The kind of activity needed to move on: acting consistently as if he fully endorsed the value he does not yet truly grasp

Therefore, it becomes almost impossible to act consistently in line with your values. You can’t act in line with two conflicting values at once. Joel fails to show up for his friends, preferring to spend the day sulking about his ex. He neglects his duties to his colleagues, because he cannot see the value in working hard to secure a future without Clementine. These behaviours align with valuing his relationship, yet that’s no longer an appropriate value behind which he can unify his perspective. But sometimes, he might take a different path and act in accordance with the value he is aware of but does not yet fully endorse: moving on. He might show up for his friends and respect his colleagues, despite often failing to see why he should bother. Perhaps we might even think that this makes him a particularly good and impressive person – rising above it.

And we’d be right, because what Joel would be doing here is precisely the kind of activity needed to move on: acting consistently as if he fully endorsed the value he does not yet truly grasp, and thereby bringing it into view. What is the nature of this as if, the engine necessary to move on?

In her book Aspiration: The Agency of Becoming (2018), Agnes Callard offers an account of this kind of activity. Aspiration is a ‘temporally extended process by which someone works to become a different and better person’. When you aspire to some value, you have an inkling of why it is valuable. But you don’t fully appreciate it, otherwise no change would be necessary for you to become the person with the value. For Callard, we do this over time by acting in response to a double ‘kind of reason’ arising from such a fractured perspective: an inkling of the potential value of a future good, fused with a recognition that our appreciation of that value is deficient.

When moving on, you lack complete knowledge of the value of having moved on – of single life, or of emotional independence, or of loving someone else. Insofar as that value is absent for you, it is possible to be motivated by the recognition that your valuational perspective is deficient. You recognise that you probably should want to move on and therefore that not wanting to move on represents a failure to appreciate that value. But this works only because you are motivated, however minimally, by the value of having moved on. It’s that flicker of motivation that gives the deficiency in your appreciation any normative force. As you gain a fuller understanding of that value, as the flicker becomes a flame, it will be less its deficiency that motivates you and more the value itself.

He starts seeking out the experiences of single life, new partners, or greater independence of mind and interests

Joel’s friends want him to get out there. But why would he get ‘out there’ when Clementine’s not ‘out there’? And yet, Joel can sense that he might be missing something, that it might be better to see that value. His friends’ persuasion appeals to this sentiment, so Joel reluctantly goes along on a night out. He doesn’t have a great time – it feels forced, like he’s pretending, dancing while fantasising about going home to Clementine. He knows he isn’t there because he wants to be, but because doing so might address the deficiency in his valuational perspective, a tentative step toward endorsing a value he knows of but doesn’t yet feel. Yet he gets something out of it, however small: a glimpse into the value of a life without Clementine, his ability to survive it, the experiences it could offer.

With time, actions of this kind expose Joel to the value he is in the process of acquiring, and he starts responding to that value itself. He starts seeking out the experiences of single life, new partners, or greater independence of mind and interests. Joel does these things less because they are a way to teach him the value of being moved on, and more because he is beginning to understand that value. He is working to address his deficient appreciation of it, and coming to recognise it for the value it holds. Aspiration, moving on, is about learning. As Callard puts it, ‘we aspire by doing things, and the things we do change us so that we are able to do the same things, or things of that kind, better and better.’

And by learning to do these things better and better, you become, in fact, a better person. Aspiration isn’t just about changing; it’s about improving. Acquiring knowledge of value, unifying yourself over time behind a consistent valuational perspective, is how you become a good person.

For consistently behaving in accordance with your values is how you constitute yourself. Every time Joel makes a choice, he will face competing, incompatible impulses of varying strength. If moving on is an active thing that Joel does, there must be some sense in which he rises above these impulses acting upon him and makes the choice himself, in a principled way. By doing that, he affirms his own agency, constituting himself as a person who does things for reasons he endorses.

Breakups splinter our values. But our job is to reunite ourselves, and get better

To do that, he must consider how he could feasibly ask anyone else, including his past and future selves, to act in relevantly similar circumstances. That means acting consistently, following his principles and values. For part of valuing something is endorsing that value, seeing it as something that should motivate someone in your situation. But it also involves showing integrity, principle and respect towards others. People with a unified valuational perspective are better able to see what is right to expect of themselves and others, and act accordingly. When your values are fractured, that’s tough. You cannot clearly see these things. Moving on is a process by which we actively bring these perspectives into view.

Things happen in our lives, like breakups, that tear us apart. But our job, as Christine Korsgaard writes in Self-Constitution (2009), is to reunify ourselves, and get better:

And in the course of this process, of falling apart and pulling yourself back together, you create something new, you constitute something new: yourself … And if you constitute yourself well, if you are good at being a person, then you’ll be a good person.

Ultimately, this is the reassurance I have taken in the difficulty of moving on. Not that I can just passively sit back, wait and, with time, I’ll get better – that is, heal. But that I can do the opposite, actively acquire a new perspective, and with time I’ll get better – that is, improve. So take steps, however small, in what may be a long journey. You can’t move anywhere in an instant. For by embarking on that journey, you’ll become a better person.

item.title: Tuesdays with the guys
item.dc:creator: Rajeev Balasubramanyam
item.description:
In the wake of an unexpected tragedy, I decided to rethink my male friendships

- by Rajeev Balasubramanyam

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Two years ago, I attended the funeral of someone I’d known who had taken his own life. He was 40 when he did it. I’d known him since he was 14, his brother one of my closest friends. The night before the funeral, I had dinner with his parents. We ate his favourite meal, a beef casserole, at the kitchen table; at one point, his siblings left the room to practise their speeches. None of them had known he was even unhappy.

At the service I met his best friend. Had he known anything was wrong?

He shook his head. ‘Not at all.’ He needed a new best man for his wedding now, he said, which was in a few weeks.

After the service, we drove off to a pub. We sat around a table with a display of our friend’s life behind us, built from old photographs his father had assembled. Several of my old friends from university were there. No one spoke at first; we were in shock. An hour and a couple of beers later, however, everyone was talking animatedly – about computer games.

I had little interest in the topic, hadn’t played one since my early 20s (Grand Theft Auto 2, which left me dreaming about chainsaws) so I wandered outside and found the friend I’d driven up with from London. He’d recently recovered from cancer, and we spoke about that before another old friend joined us. Later, we went inside to look at the photographs. Many were of the deceased as a child. I found it hard to look at the ones where he was playing with his toddler. I’d become a father recently, too.

For days afterwards, two questions kept returning to my mind: why hadn’t he told anyone he was unhappy? And why, in the face of overwhelming grief, were grown men talking about computer games?

All the men I knew had serious problems to cope with. My close friend Mark, whose brother’s funeral I’d attended, was struggling. He’d just moved to Canada too, where he knew nobody. There was my friend James who’d recovered from cancer; both his parents had died within six months of one another. We had another mutual friend, Howard, whose father was dying. He and I often watched cricket together but, as much as we loved the game, maybe this was a way of not talking about the things that really mattered – just like the computer game talk at the pub. That too seemed to me a way of denying the pain and sorrow we were all feeling, which was ludicrous given that we were at a funeral… of a man who hadn’t talked about his feelings.

I called up my three friends and announced: we were going to start a men’s group.

Among the four of us, I was the only one used to this kind of thing. I’d been going to spiritual retreats for years, had cried in several sharing circles (mostly in California). The first time, at a monastery outside San Diego, I’d barely said a word, watching in silence while others cried freely. Since then, I’d cried all night on ayahuasca retreats, told strangers details about my life I’d rarely shared with anyone. But this was different. We were old friends, had related to one another in the same way for 30 years. Would we be able to connect in a different register? I hoped they’d at least consider it.

Our second problem was location. For a start, we lived in four different countries, which meant we’d have to meet online. Mark lived in Vancouver. James was in London, Howard in Brussels, and I lived in Berlin. Scheduling would be tricky. When I pitched the idea, however, the reaction was unanimous: all three of them were in, without reservation. I think I had underestimated the need.

There were nerves, however. When I created a WhatsApp group, one of them quipped: ‘Are we supposed to talk about hunting and power tools?’ He was embarrassed, I supposed. We weren’t used to consciously being men. What did that even mean?

My idea was that each of us could take it in turns to talk while the others listened

‘A few ground rules,’ I said, at the start of our first gathering. ‘Can we please try to make it a few minutes early for each session?’

‘You’re being very bossy, Rajeev,’ said Howard.

‘It’s because you don’t work for a company,’ said James. ‘You’re not used to meetings.’

‘Why don’t we just start the meet at 8.02?’ said Howard. ‘Then we’re early if we’re on time.’

‘You’ll get used to it,’ said Mark. ‘We’ll all cancel at the last minute anyway with some ridiculous excuse.’

I took a few breaths. I just wanted to make sure we got the most out of the sessions, I explained. My idea was that each of us could take it in turns to talk while the others listened. Afterwards, we would ask questions or comment but, crucially, refrain from giving advice.

‘Hey,’ said Howard. ‘Did you hear that…?’

Jim Gordon – the drummer from Derek and the Dominos (Eric Clapton’s old group) – who’d murdered his mother with a hammer and a butcher’s knife, had died in prison.

‘What?’ said Mark. ‘Hold on, let me Google this.’

‘Did he play with Joe Cocker?’ said James.

‘And Crosby, Stills and Nash, apparently.’

‘And the Incredible Bongo Band.’

I was very close to screaming now.

‘Can we please stop talking about this,’ I said.

Everyone looked up, as if waking from a dream.

‘OK, we’d better stop, Rajeev’s getting annoyed,’ said James.

‘Sorry, Rajeev,’ said Mark.

‘We don’t want to annoy Rajeev,’ said Howard.

I knew they were making fun of me, but I decided to take it on the chin: the fate of the organiser.

In the first session, I offered to go first, knowing that if I was open and vulnerable, the others would find it easier in turn. Luckily, I’d had a terrible week. My agent had responded with scorn to a very honest and revealing draft of a memoir I was working on, and my confidence was in tatters. I told the group this, somewhat awkward and shy myself, and when I’d finished, I suggested we move on to the next person.

‘Too many questions,’ said Howard.

‘I’m so sorry this happened,’ said James. ‘That’s so hard.’

‘What’s really sad is that you’ve lost your confidence,’ said Howard.

After I’d spoken, the others were very open, as I’d hoped they would be

We continued like this for 10 minutes. There was no analysis; I didn’t figure out a way forward in that time. Perhaps the best word for it was connection. I just felt held.

After I’d spoken, the others were very open, as I’d hoped they would be. James told us he’d thought he wouldn’t have much to say, but the reality was he’d been struggling after the death of his parents.

‘I realise now that I’m not as fine as I thought I was,’ he said.

This wasn’t a negative thing. It meant he was feeling more connected to himself.

We continued like this for a year. Howard’s father died, and we devoted the entire session to him. He’d needed this, he said. All he’d been doing was administrative formalities, the dreaded ‘deadmin’, as it’s called. He’d hardly had time to feel, let alone talk about his feelings. James sympathised. He’d been going through this for months, the endless bureaucracy and phone calls.

Another time, Howard admitted he’d been experiencing some pain in his knees. He couldn’t run anymore, was worried about it.

‘Howard,’ said Mark, raising his hand in paternal, dictatorial fashion. ‘No excuses. First, go to the doctor. Second…’

James seconded this, adding further lifestyle injunctions, while Howard nodded, his expression increasingly penitent, if not sheepish, before I intervened.

‘Can we please try not to give each other advice?’ I said. ‘And not to lay down the law. Let’s just listen and ask questions. I mean, if you really want to, it’s OK, but let’s try to be gentle.’

The entire reason for the group was to be ourselves together: messy, frightened and overwhelmed

Everyone looked surprised. This was the way we’d been brought up, the way that we, as men, were used to talking, but they agreed. Sometimes, someone would begin a sentence with: ‘We’re not supposed to give each other advice, so…’ and rethink what they wanted to say. It made me wonder if I was being dictatorial myself with this injunction but decided to do it anyway. We were learning a new way of communicating and, for the most part, it was working.

When I’d had a relatively smooth week, being the organiser was easy. Sometimes, however, I was reluctant to tell them how I was feeling because I didn’t want to take up too much space, or to be a burden to anyone. If they were struggling, I didn’t want to make it even harder for them. Gradually however, I came to realise there was no point in trying to hide or pretend. The entire reason for the group’s inception was that we could be ourselves together: messy, frightened and overwhelmed, which was how we all felt much of the time.

Perhaps this is obvious, but it was through our men’s group that I realised an eternal truth: everyone has problems, and the problems just keep on coming. Anyone who claimed otherwise was probably lying, which I did every day, particularly with people I didn’t know well or didn’t trust.

In fact, I would argue that the most dangerous thing we can do with our problems is to keep them to ourselves, which, unfortunately, is what men tend to do. I lost another friend to suicide recently, one I hadn’t heard from in years, though I’d tried to get in touch. I wonder whether, if he’d had a group like we do, he’d still be with us today. Our group doesn’t fix our problems; all it does is act as a safety net, a way of ensuring that bad experiences don’t become traumas, frustrations don’t become depressions, and legitimate worries don’t end up as despair, or desperation. And this may, in the end, be the difference between living and dying.

item.title: Want to be a lifelong learner? Don’t go it alone
item.dc:creator: Celine Nguyen
item.description:
The history of autodidacticism shows that learning has always been social. The right relationships open intellectual horizons

- by Celine Nguyen

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The year after I graduated from university – from a degree that I struggled through dutifully and mostly dispassionately – I began to feel that I had missed out on an actual education. Like many other students, I’d entered university keenly aware of high tuition fees and the threat of student loans and, as a result, I often chose classes based on the employment opportunities they offered. But once I graduated and secured a job, I found myself returning to the interests I had abandoned along the way: literature, art, history, philosophy. I wanted to understand the ideas and events that had shaped the world around me. And I wanted to, like the thinkers I admired, use historical anecdotes to analyse a contemporary event, or put different novels and artworks in conversation with each other. Could I teach myself to do the same?

The internet is full of resources for self-directed learning: for any subject, you can easily find blog posts about essential texts, links to university syllabi, and hours of YouTube lectures. When I attempted to make use of these guides, however, I often found myself disengaged and unfocused. I chastised myself for scrolling through social media while watching online lectures, or forgetting most of the ideas inside the books I read.

The problem, however, wasn’t my attention span. It was my approach: I was struggling because I saw learning as a solitary pursuit.

What formal education institutions offer is a community where students learn from both professors and their peers. But universities aren’t the only places where these relationships are built. The historian Jonathan Rose’s history of autodidactism from the 18th to 20th centuries, The Intellectual Life of the British Working Classes (2001), shows how those with little to no formal education can cultivate rich intellectual lives. Rose draws from memoirs written by miners, weavers, labourers and housemaids, which vividly depict the kind of social structures that can help people learn. I was surprised and gratified to find that self-study didn’t require isolation. In 18th-century Scotland, for example, miners founded libraries where members pooled their annual subscription fees to buy books. These libraries were often associated with ‘mutual improvement’ meetings, where working-class men could learn from each other. ‘At each meeting,’ Rose writes:

One member would deliver a paper on any imaginable subject – politics, literature, religion, ethics, ‘useful knowledge’ – and then the topic would be thrown open to general discussion. The aim was to develop the verbal and intellectual skills of people who had never been encouraged to speak or think.

Learning is better understood, they suggested, as a highly collaborative social practice

Rose’s autodidacts weren’t just learning about other people’s ideas. They were also learning to take their own ideas seriously. ‘There was complete freedom of expression,’ Rose observes; ‘the teacher-pupil hierarchy was abolished, and costs were minimal.’ Many of the people involved were seeking knowledge for knowledge’s sake, but the education they received – from books, and from each other – often shaped them into social reformers and political radicals. Francis Place, for example, was a tailor whose formal education consisted of a single spelling book. He later became a strike leader, birth-control advocate, and an organiser for the London Corresponding Library (which lent books and organised weekly meetings for members). His memoir, published only posthumously in 1972, describes the library’s impact on its working-class members:

It induced men to read books, instead of wasting their time … it taught them to respect themselves, and to desire to educate their children. It elevated them in their own opinions … [and] elevated them in society.

I was touched by Place’s words, which reflected what I wanted from my own education: self-respect, more meaningful ways to spend my time, and an enlarged sense of how to contribute to the world. And I began to see how self-directed learning required more than just the self. The most influential forms, it seemed, involved dedicated communities – what the anthropologist Jean Lave and the educational theorist Etienne Wenger call ‘communities of practice’ in their book Situated Learning (1991). Conventional models of learning tend to focus on individuals, who are assumed to merely internalise knowledge from others. But Lave and Wenger’s ethnographic study of five different communities – ‘midwives, tailors, quartermasters, butchers, non-drinking alcoholics’ – drawn together by a shared profession or passion, led to different conclusions. Learning is better understood, they suggested, as a highly collaborative social practice.

I was also relieved to discover that the people whom Rose, Lave and Wenger studied often made do without teachers. The mutual improvement societies Rose describes show how gratifying peer-to-peer relationships can be. And even among communities of practice where people were formally apprenticed to a more experienced professional, Lave and Wenger found that there was ‘very little observable teaching’ – apprentices often learned from each other, not just from their superiors.

This is good news for learners who haven’t found a teacher or knowledgeable mentor yet. And it suggests that, even in a formal educational environment, the best teachers are those who promote egalitarianism over hierarchical learning.

My interest in self-directed learning eventually led me to the Brazilian philosopher Paulo Freire, one of the most influential educational theorists of the 20th century. In his impassioned manifesto Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968), he criticised the idea that ‘the teacher teaches and the students are taught … the teacher knows everything and the students know nothing.’ True learning, Freire believed, could be accomplished only ‘through the restless, impatient, continuing, hopeful inquiry human beings pursue in the world, with the world, and with each other.’

One way to describe Freire’s philosophy, Daniel Walden writes, is that ‘the teacher is not so much an authority as a more experienced student.’ This seems like a radical redescription of what teachers are meant to do in the classroom.

More experienced students can show newer ones what it’s like to be generous to your peers and open to new perspectives

Walden is a classicist who began his career teaching the ‘Great Books’: foundational works of Western literature and philosophy, often emphasising Greek, Roman and biblical texts. In a recent essay in The Point magazine, Walden suggests that Freire’s educational approach closely reflects his own goals as a teacher of the Iliad, the Odyssey, the tragedies of Aeschylus and other classical texts – even those he doesn’t know particularly well. ‘My own teaching benefits tremendously from being unable to pretend to any kind of expertise,’ he writes; ‘texts outside my disciplinary wheelhouse have become some of my favourite material to teach precisely because I can explore them alongside my students rather than insisting that I have something they need.’ Of course, Walden isn’t quite like the students he teaches because he’s spent years studying subjects that others are approaching for the first time. But by demonstrating his own intellectual humility and curiosity, he can invite students to embody these traits too. More experienced students can show newer ones what it’s like to be generous to your peers and open to new perspectives. ‘The secret ingredient,’ Walden writes, ‘is not only the syllabus but the intellectual community that is formed.’

Walden’s description resonated with me because I had experienced this myself: an intellectual community that helped me, and my peers, explore new ideas together.

Seven years after graduating from university, I signed up for a philosophy class taught by the poet Zoe Tuck. In our weekly Zoom conversations, Tuck acted less like a superior than a charismatic, encouraging peer. We read Maurice Merleau-Ponty’s Phenomenology of Perception (1945) together, slowly working through passages that exhilarated and perplexed us. Some people in the group had formally studied philosophy, but many hadn’t. Together, we learned to approach the text with the right balance of humility, confidence and curiosity. And we learned, too, what it meant to pursue self-directed learning in a community.

I had moved from the passive experience of reading a book to the more receptive, social practice of discussing it with others. But I wanted an even more active, generative education: I wanted to produce new works and forms of knowledge. In a university setting, this typically takes place when students need to submit a significant project or thesis. Where else could I find models for self-directed learning? This question led me to stories where someone’s intellectual interests helped launch an unexpected creative career. When J R R Tolkien and C S Lewis first met in 1926, neither man had written the novels that made them famous. Instead, Tolkien was a professor in the English department at the University of Oxford, who had published scholarly works in a small niche, and Lewis was a departmental fellow. The two became closer after realising that they both loved reading Nordic poetry, even though it was unrelated to their research.

A formal education is, for many, only the beginning of one’s intellectual and creative life

A year earlier, Tolkien had shown his mentor an epic poem he was working on, inspired by Norse mythology. His mentor wasn’t particularly supportive, and ‘advised him to drop it’, as the sociologist Michael P Farrell notes in Collaborative Circles (2001), his study of creative friendships. Tolkien resolved to keep his poem a secret. But when he worked up the courage to share it with Lewis, he received a remarkably supportive response: warm praise, along with detailed feedback about specific lines. Being encouraged by a peer may have healed some of the insecurities of being rejected by a superior. As Tolkien gratefully observed:

The unpayable debt that I owe to him was not influence as it is ordinarily understood, but sheer encouragement. He was for long my only audience. Only from him did I ever get the idea that my stuff could be more than a private hobby.

The two began reading each other’s drafts in a critique group that eventually grew to seven members. Two widely read and beloved fiction series eventually emerged from this group: Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings (1954-55) and Lewis’s The Chronicles of Narnia (1950-56). Today, both men are remembered for their novels, not their earlier academic careers.

In the first few years of my self-directed education, I envied those who seemed to have the ideal formal education, complete with the right professors, peers and structure. But stories like these helped me realise that a formal education is, for many, only the beginning of one’s intellectual and creative life. I began, slowly but surely, to piece together what my own intellectual life looked like: taking online classes with writers and literary scholars; joining in-person book clubs to deepen my understanding of challenging texts; and finding friends who offered generous, useful feedback on my work.

Relationships like these might be the most important resource for learning something new. You can teach yourself almost anything, it turns out, within a community of encouraging and intellectually ambitious peers.

item.title: A psychological guide to climbing out of debt
item.dc:creator: Vicky Reynal
item.description:
Debt is as much an emotional challenge as a financial one. Follow this therapist’s advice to create a plan that works

- by Vicky Reynal

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
If you’re struggling with debt, you’ll know that it is more than a financial issue. As a psychotherapist, I work every day with people who have ended up in problem debt – debt that is a struggle to manage or pay back, leading to a spiralling financial situation. I’ve seen firsthand how often debt has roots in deeply emotional issues – and I’ve witnessed its emotional consequences.

Many clients have told me they associate debt with being ‘disorganised’ and feeling ‘irresponsible’. They feel shame about what their debt ‘makes them’ and fear that seeking help will lead to them being judged negatively. As a result, even talking about it becomes difficult. Of course, debt can result from irresponsible behaviour, but this is far from always the case. Anyone can end up with problem debt as a result of relationship breakdown, redundancy, illness and other practical hardships. Whatever the root causes, it can be difficult to face.

You may have found that simple tasks like checking your banking app or opening letters from the bank, calling the bank or seeking money advice feel impossible, perhaps out of a fear of judgment or seeing how the debt has grown. But the longer debt goes unaddressed, the worse the consequences – not just financial (the earlier debt is tackled the more options there are), but also emotional. Guilt can turn into a pervasive shame; a small secret kept long can break the trust in relationships. The manageable becomes overwhelming.

So climbing out of debt isn’t just a financial task, but one that requires the emotional capacity to face the fact without collapsing into panic or avoidance; the courage to take action (action breeds confidence rather than the other way round); the curiosity to explore what caused the debt in the first place; and the humility to ask for help.

I have been with clients as they revealed debt to their partners, and slowly rebuilt those relationships. I have heard their relief when they called the bank and were met with understanding rather than punishment. I have seen first-hand how empowered they felt once the barrier of avoidance is broken. Debt feels terminal, but it doesn’t have to be. It is a problem to be faced, not something that defines you.

I help my clients to unpack what led them to this place and also to find a way out of the shame, dread and secrecy that usually accompanies debt. Below are my suggestions for how you too can find the emotional resources to climb out of your debt.

item.title: S P A C E S
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
A filmmaker tries to reconstruct her brother’s faltering experience of time: adrift and without continuity

- Directed by Nora Štrbová

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: To what extent is our identity intertwined with our memory? The Prague-based filmmaker Nora Štrbová explores this hazy terrain in her mixed-media animation S P A C E S. The film is based on the life of her brother Šimon, who developed a brain tumour that gradually eroded his memory before ultimately taking his life in his 20s. Fragmented visual sequences, including reimagined moments from Šimon’s life and an interview with his friend, break apart and blur, evoking her brother’s faltering experience of time – and, by extension, his faltering experience of himself. Inventive and poignant in equal measure, Štrbová’s immersive short finds a deeper meaning and emotional pull through this experimentation.
